title: Bloom Filters
tagline: Probabilistic membership in O(k) time and constant space — false positives are possible, false negatives are impossible.

sections.content:
A **Bloom filter** is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure that answers membership queries — "have I seen this item before?" — with a deliberate trade-off: it may occasionally say "yes" when the correct answer is "no" (a **false positive**), but it will **never** say "no" when the correct answer is "yes" (no false negatives). That asymmetry is the entire design.

A Bloom filter uses a **bit array** of m bits and **k independent hash functions**. Each function maps any input to one of the m bit positions. To insert an element, set the k corresponding bits. To query, check all k bits — if every bit is 1, the element is **probably** in the set; if any bit is 0, the element is **definitely not** in the set. No element is ever stored, so a Bloom filter uses constant space relative to the number of insertions — a hash set by comparison grows linearly. This makes Bloom filters invaluable in cache layers, network routing, database optimisations, and anywhere the cost of a false negative is catastrophic but a false positive is merely inconvenient.

sections.caption: Inserting 'cat' sets bits 2, 5, 9. Querying 'dog' checks h1('dog')=1 — bit[1] is 0, so 'dog' is definitely not in the set.

sections.title: A Nightclub Bouncer with a Punch Card
sections.content:
Imagine a nightclub bouncer who cannot remember every person they have ever seen but carries a punchcard with 1 000 holes and 3 coloured stamps. When someone enters, the bouncer stamps three positions on the card (determined by the person's face, name, and birthday — the three hash functions). When someone claims to have visited before, the bouncer checks those three positions: if all three are stamped, they are "probably" a returning guest; if even one is unstamped, they have definitely never visited.

The catch: after enough guests, many positions overlap. A new person's three positions might all happen to be stamped by different past guests — a **false positive**. The bouncer waves them in even though they are a first-time visitor. But a genuine returning guest always has their three positions stamped — no false negatives. The larger the punchcard (more bits), the lower the false-positive rate; more stamps per person (more hash functions) can help or hurt depending on the fill level.

The **false-positive rate** of a Bloom filter with m bits, n inserted elements, and k hash functions is approximately:

`FPR ≈ (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k`

For given m and n, the optimal number of hash functions that minimises FPR is `k = (m/n) × ln(2) ≈ 0.693 × (m/n)`. The optimal bit-per-element ratio for a target FPR of p is `m/n = -log₂(p) / ln(2) ≈ 1.44 × log₂(1/p)`. To achieve 1% FPR you need about 9.6 bits per element with ~7 hash functions — compare this to storing full 64-byte strings in a hash set.

A Bloom filter can never remove elements because clearing a bit might affect other elements that share it. **Counting Bloom filters** extend each bit to a small counter, enabling deletion at the cost of 3–4× more space. **Cuckoo filters** are a modern alternative that support deletion with similar space efficiency.

**Classic applications**:
- **Web crawlers** (Google, early) check whether a URL has been crawled before without storing all URLs in memory.
- **Database query optimisation**: before a disk-expensive join, check the Bloom filter of the inner table — if the key definitely does not exist, skip the disk read.
- **Distributed caches** (Redis, Cassandra): check whether a key possibly exists before a cache miss round-trip.
- **Malware / phishing detection**: browsers check URLs against a Bloom filter of known-bad URLs stored locally — no false negatives means no phishing URL is ever missed.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Double hashing `h1 + i×h2` generates k pseudo-independent positions from two base hashes — avoids the cost of k independent hash functions. Bits are packed 8 per byte using bitwise operations. `fillRatio` shows how many bits are set — a high fill ratio (> 0.5) means increasing false-positive risk and suggests the filter is undersized.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The sizing formulas let you calculate exactly how large to make a Bloom filter before deployment. 1% FPR costs 9.6 bits per element with 7 hash functions — a fixed, predictable cost regardless of element size. A hash set's cost scales with element size (strings, URLs can be 50–200 bytes each).

sections.content: **The defining property of a Bloom filter is: false negatives are impossible.** If `mightContain()` returns `false`, you have a mathematical guarantee the element was never inserted. This asymmetry is what makes Bloom filters safe for cache guards: you might do an unnecessary cache miss (false positive) but you will never skip a valid cached item (false negative would be a bug). When an interviewer asks about Bloom filters, immediately state both properties — no false negatives, possible false positives — and the typical use case: 'fast first-pass filter before an expensive exact lookup'.

items: A Bloom filter uses a bit array of m bits and k hash functions; insert sets k bits, query checks k bits — both O(k) operations with O(m) space.
False negatives are impossible: a 'not present' answer is always correct. False positives are possible: a 'present' answer means 'probably present'.
False-positive rate depends on m (bits), n (insertions), and k (hashes): FPR ≈ (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. More bits and optimal k minimise FPR.
Standard Bloom filters do not support deletion — clearing a bit could break other elements. Counting Bloom filters and Cuckoo filters add deletion support.
Applications: URL deduplication in web crawlers, database join optimisation, distributed cache guards, browser malware detection, and username-availability checks.

quiz.question: What does a Bloom filter guarantee about 'not present' answers?
options: They may be wrong — false negatives are possible
They are always correct — if mightContain returns false the element was definitely never inserted
They are correct 99% of the time depending on the hash functions
They are only correct when the filter is less than 50% full
quiz.explanation: If any of the k bits is 0, the element was definitely not inserted — because insertion always sets all k bits. A 'not present' result is always correct: zero false negatives. Only 'present' answers can be wrong (false positives).

quiz.question: What causes a false positive in a Bloom filter?
options: A hash function collision that maps two different inputs to the same output
All k bit positions of a queried element happen to be set by combinations of prior insertions
The bit array becomes full and cannot store new information
Two elements share the same first hash function output
quiz.explanation: A false positive occurs when all k bit positions for a new element are already 1 — not because that element was inserted, but because those positions were set by different previously inserted elements. No single element needs to share all k positions; the overlap can come from multiple distinct insertions.

quiz.question: Why can standard Bloom filters not support deletion?
options: Deletion is slower than O(k) due to bit propagation
Clearing the k bits for one element might clear bits that are also set by other elements, causing false negatives
The hash functions are not reversible, so the bits cannot be located
Bloom filters do not store elements, so deletion has no effect
quiz.explanation: Multiple elements can share individual bit positions. Clearing element A's bits might clear a bit that element B also set. Future queries for B would then return false — a false negative — violating the core guarantee. Counting Bloom filters solve this by using counters instead of bits.

quiz.question: What is the effect of increasing the number of bits m (while keeping n and k fixed) on false-positive rate?
options: FPR increases — more bits means more collisions
FPR stays the same — only k affects FPR
FPR decreases — bits are less densely set, reducing accidental matches
FPR becomes 0 — no false positives with enough bits
quiz.explanation: More bits means the n×k set operations are spread over a larger array, so individual bits are less likely to be set. The fill ratio (fraction of set bits) drops, and the probability that all k positions for a new element are accidentally set decreases.

quiz.question: For n=1 000 000 elements and a target 1% false-positive rate, approximately how many bits per element does an optimally sized Bloom filter need?
options: 1 bit per element
4 bits per element
9.6 bits per element
64 bits per element
quiz.explanation: The formula m/n = -log₂(p)/ln(2) gives m/n = log₂(100)/ln(2) ≈ 6.64/0.693 ≈ 9.58 bits per element for 1% FPR. A hash set storing 50-byte average-length keys uses 400 bits per element — about 40× more space.

quiz.question: Which use case is a Bloom filter UNSUITABLE for?
options: Checking whether a URL has been crawled before in a web crawler
Filtering database lookups to avoid disk reads for definitely-absent keys
Storing the exact set of all registered usernames for authentication
Detecting known malicious URLs in a browser extension
quiz.explanation: Authentication cannot tolerate false positives — if a Bloom filter incorrectly says a username exists, a new user is wrongly rejected. Authentication requires exact membership (use a hash set or database). Bloom filters are only appropriate when false positives are a minor inconvenience, not a correctness bug.

quiz.question: What is double hashing in the context of Bloom filters?
options: Hashing each element twice through the same hash function
Using two base hash functions h1 and h2 to derive k positions via g_i(x) = h1(x) + i*h2(x) mod m
Storing each element in two separate bit arrays for redundancy
Applying SHA-256 twice to increase collision resistance
quiz.explanation: Double hashing generates k pseudo-independent bit positions from just two hash function evaluations: g_i(x) = (h1(x) + i × h2(x)) mod m for i = 0, 1, ..., k-1. This is far cheaper than computing k truly independent hash functions and has been proven to maintain near-optimal Bloom filter properties.

quiz.question: A Bloom filter is 80% full (80% of bits are set to 1). What is the consequence?
options: New insertions will fail because there is no more space
False-positive rate rises sharply — most queries for unseen elements will accidentally find all k bits set
The filter automatically resizes to accommodate more elements
False-negative rate increases proportionally
quiz.explanation: FPR ≈ (fill_ratio)^k. At 80% fill with k=7 hashes: (0.8)^7 ≈ 0.21 — a 21% false-positive rate, far above the intended design. Bloom filters should be sized so fill ratio stays below ~50% under expected load.

quiz.question: How do Cuckoo filters improve on standard Bloom filters?
options: They use fewer hash functions, reducing computational cost
They support deletion and achieve similar or better space efficiency
They eliminate false positives entirely
They store actual elements alongside the bit array
quiz.explanation: Cuckoo filters store small fingerprints of elements in a cuckoo hash table. This allows deletion (remove the fingerprint) with comparable or better space efficiency than Bloom filters at low FPR. Standard Bloom filters cannot delete; counting Bloom filters can but use 3–4× more space.

quiz.question: Chrome's Safe Browsing feature stores a Bloom filter of known malicious URLs locally. Why is this an appropriate use of a Bloom filter?
options: Exact matches are required — no false positives are acceptable in security
The filter must be queried on every network request — O(k) speed is critical and false positives only cause an extra server round-trip
Bloom filters allow the browser to store URLs and their page content
Bloom filters can be updated without re-downloading the filter
quiz.explanation: Chrome checks every URL against a local Bloom filter before making a network request to Google's servers. False positives (innocent URLs mistakenly flagged) only cause a single extra server round-trip to confirm. False negatives (real malicious URL not caught) are prevented by the no-false-negative guarantee. This makes Bloom filters perfect: fast local check, no missed threats.
